title: TA9-23401
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the male claimant) and his wife, XXXX XXXX (the female claimant) allege to be citizens of the People's Republic of China (China), who also hold permanent resident status in Panama. Their three adult children, XXXX XXXX XXXX (24 years old), XXXX XXXX XXXX (22 years old) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (21 years old) (the co-claimants), are citizens of Panama. They claim refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1 ALLEGATIONS

The Personal Information Form (PIF)2 narrative of the female claimant was adopted by all of the claimants. In her PIF narrative, she stated that she immigrated to Panama in 1988. She met her husband there and together they had three children. Beginning in 1992, they began to be harassed and robbed on a regular basis. In XXXX 1992, robbers broke into their store and forced them to give money at gunpoint. Though they went to the police, their complaint was not registered. In 1993, their store was robbed again. The police were called but they did not take a written report. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2001, the male and female claimants were asleep in their bed and were awoken by two armed masked men. The female claimant was raped. All the valuables were taken from their home. They found out later that the landlord upstairs had also been robbed. The police were called and took their statement. They did not hear from the police again. The female claimant felt anxiety and stress after this and in XXXX 2001, she became a Christian. On XXXX XXXX, 2008, armed robbers broke into their store and their relative who was working there was shot and killed. The police asked them to identify the criminals from a list of photographs but they were unable to do so. After they reopened their store the next week, they received a telephoned threat telling them not to assist the police or they would be killed. They received other threatening calls. They decided to leave Panama. They allege that they cannot return to China because of the birth control policy and because of their religion. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimants' testimony and the supporting documentation filed3 establish the male and female claimants' identities as nationals of China with permanent residence status in Panama. Passports for the three co-claimants establish their identities as citizens of Panama.

The Refugee Protection Division finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The panel is not persuaded that the claimants have grounds for fearing persecution. The panel also concludes that the claimants are not persons in need of protection pursuant to subsections 97(1)(a) or (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Exclusion
The panel has considered whether the male and female claimants should be excluded under section 1E of the Refugee Convention pursuant to section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

Section E of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees states: This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

There are four criteria that the Board should follow in undertaking an analysis of whether a claimants enjoy the "basic rights" attached to the possession of nationality in the country to residents: (i) the right to return to the country of residence; (ii) the right to work freely without restrictions; (iii) the right to study; and (iv) full access to social services in the country of residence.

In addition, if the claimant has some sort of temporary status which must be renewed and which could be cancelled, or if the claimant does not have the right to return to the country of residence, the claimant should not be excluded under Article 1E.4 However, a temporary status which must be renewed which could be cancelled can be sufficient for the application of Article 1E exclusion. In this regard, it should be noted that even a Canadian permanent resident could have their status revoked if they reside outside of Canada for more than six months. Even in Canada there are no unconditional rights to permanent resident.5

The claimants state that they have permanent resident status in Panama and this status was not contested by counsel at the hearing or in her submissions. The claimants resided in Panama for over 20 years. They have submitted into evidence their indefinite work permits6 and voter cards.7 Having considered that the male and female claimants have permanent resident status in Panama, as well as their personal circumstances and their lifestyle in that country, I find that they are excluded under article 1E. Panama

The panel has considered the allegations made by all of the claimants that they cannot return to Panama because they would be persecuted and subjected to serious harm. They have stated that they have been threatened and seriously harmed by gangsters and robbers in Panama and that they were not protected by the Panamanian government. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that that the claimants have been victims of crime in Panama. The female claimant stated that she was raped in the course of a robbery at their home in 2001. In assessing her claim, the panel has considered the Chairperson's Guidelines on Gender-Related Persecution.8 The Chairperson's Guidelines highlight that women refugee claimants may face special problems in demonstrating that their claims are credible and trustworthy. Factors that may affect their ability to provide evidence include difficulty in providing testimony on sensitive matters, cross-cultural misunderstandings as well as social, religious and economic differences. The Chairperson's Guidelines were used to help understand and apply the added sensitivities necessary to properly assess whether any credibility issues are the result of such difficulties or an attempt to fabricate evidence. A female panel was provided for the hearing. The panel acknowledges that the rape was an extremely traumatic experience which the female claimant stated she dealt with by turning to Christianity. Having considered the circumstances of this crime, the panel concludes that she was the victim of a criminal act. The panel notes that the rape occurred in 2001 and that there were no such incidents in the subsequent years that she remained in Panama.

The Federal Court has held that victims of crime, corruption9 or vendettas10 generally fail to establish any link between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds and the Immigration and Refugee Board (the Board) has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of any personal vendetta or where the claimant was a victim of crime.11 The claimants, in this circumstance, fear serious harm by common criminals according to the written narrative and oral testimony. They have stated in their testimony and in their PIF narrative that they were robbed many times at their place of business and at their home, that the female claimant was raped in 2001 during a robbery at their home, that an employee was murdered at their place of business in 2008 during a robbery and that they were threatened not to go to the police. At the hearing, all of the claimants testified that they feared criminality in Panama. The claimants presented documentary evidence,12 which consisted of newspaper clippings, intended to indicate that persons of Chinese background are targets of criminals committing robbery. However, the claimants did not indicate how these crimes compare to other rates of robbery or homicide occurring within the general population of Panama. There is no evidence before the panel that the assailants were known to the claimants or that the assailants recognized the claimants. I find that the claimants have failed to provide sufficient and trustworthy evidence to demonstrate that the incidents were not random criminal acts perpetrated by criminals. It is reasonable to conclude that the claimants were frightened and traumatized by the incidents that happened, however the evidence did not persuade the panel that the claimants were specifically targeted due to their ethnicity. The claimants stated at the hearing that because they owned a business that served the public criminals perceived them to have money. As well, the panel notes from the articles submitted into documentary evidence that perpetrators of these crimes have been arrested. Further, the documentary evidence in the IRB National Documentation Package13 notes that many of the Chinese businesses are located in 'high crime areas' and that the police are taking action to counter the issue. A delegation from the Chinese Association of Panama also "complained that many of their businesses serve high crime areas and don't get very much police protection" (Panama News 1 Oct. 2009). However, the National Police of Panama (Policía Nacional de Panamá, PNP) has established a program called "Comercios Vigilantes" (Vigilant Businesses) in commercial sectors as a way to prevent crime; its success depends on the participation and coordination of employees, owners, customers and the public (Panama n.d.).

The panel concludes the police are making serious attempts to provide the protection the public in Panama might expect. The panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that the fear in this case is not linked to race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group. Therefore, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants' fear is as victims of generalized crime that could befall any individual in Panama. The panel will also examine whether adequate state protection is available to the claimants should they return to Panama. Alternate Analysis
Alternately, for the reasons that follow, I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugee nor persons in need of protection. State Protection

Panama is a representative democracy with three branches of government: executive and legislative branches elected by direct vote for five-year terms, and an appointed judiciary. An autonomous Electoral Tribunal supervises voter registration, the election process, and the activities of political parties. The judiciary is independent of the executive and the legislature. The judicial branch (justices) is appointed by the head of state. The judicial branch is organized under a nine-member Supreme Court (each judge is appointed for a 10-year term) and includes all tribunals and municipal courts. As of July 2010, the Panamanian Security Forces consisted of the Panamanian National Police (PNP), the National Frontier Service (Servicio Nacional de Fronteras or SENAFRONT), the National Aero-Naval Service (Servicio Nacional Aero-Naval or SENAN), and the Institutional Protection Service (SPI--a secret service equivalent).14 Civilian authorities in the new Ministry of Public Security (formed on April 1 from the Ministry of Government and Justice) maintained effective control over all police, investigative, border, air, and maritime forces in the country, which has no regular military forces.15 The PNP remains responsible for internal law enforcement and public order. The government has effective mechanisms to investigate and punish abuse and corruption.16

The law criminalizes rape, including spousal rape, with prison terms of five to 10 years, or eight to 10 years under aggravating circumstances (use of a weapon), and the government enforced the law effectively. Rapes constituted the majority of sexual crimes investigated by the PNP and its Directorate of Judicial Investigation reported 1,030 cases of rape in the context of domestic violence during the year.17 There is an Office of the Ombudsman (Defensoria del Pueblo), which allows the public to complain with respect to human rights issues.18 The Ombudsman receives complaints against the police for abuse of authority. Freedom of assembly is recognized, and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) are free to operate.19

A state, unless in complete breakdown, is presumed capable of protecting its citizens.20 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board, on the balance of probabilities, that the evidence supports such allegations.21 The claimant's evidentiary burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to her.22 Panama is a parliamentary democracy whose citizens have the right to change their government through free and fair elections.23 The government generally respects the rights of its citizens.24 The law provides for an independent judiciary.25 The Constitution provides for freedom of speech and expression, rights that the government generally respected.26 A wide variety of domestic and international human rights groups generally operated without government restriction, investigating abuses and publishing their findings on human rights cases.27

Based on the foregoing, I find that Panama does have the apparatus necessary to provide adequate protection to its citizens. It is also clear from the documentary evidence before the panel that problems do exist at a number of levels of government and police. Documentary evidence further indicates that the government of Panama does not provide perfect protection to its citizens28 but it appears to be taking steps to improve its system. In consideration of the totality of the evidence before me, I find, pursuant to the principles set out in Villafranca,29 that the Panamanian government does make serious efforts to protect its citizens and the mere fact that it is not always successful in doing so does not rebut the presumption of state protection.

The objective evidence regarding state protection is mixed and as such does not constitute clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection. I have considered the claimants' evidence regarding state protection. The claimants in this instance fear victimization by individuals who have allegedly robbed their business and family of personal property and seriously harmed the female claimant. The claimants stated in their testimony and PIF narrative that every time an incident happened, they called the police. The male claimant was asked at the hearing whether he had any police reports to corroborate that the police were contacted each time there was a robbery or incident. He stated that the police did not give them reports. He was asked if he had contacted the police to inquire if they had reports. He replied that the police had told him that if they had any information they would let him know. The male claimant was asked again if he had contacted the police in Panama regarding acquiring reports. He replied that he had not. He was asked why he had not contacted the police to get reports to corroborate his allegations. He responded that at the time he was fearful and that sometimes the police would bring by a big picture book. He was asked whether he had made any attempt after he arrived in Canada to contact the police to see if they had reports. He replied that the police just took notes. He was asked how he knew that the police did not make a report at the police station. He stated that he didn't know why he needed a report. It was pointed out to the male claimant that he had been asked in the Screening Form and in the instructions for the completion of his PIF to provide documentation to corroborate his story, which included police documentation. He replied that he had provided his relative's death certificate. He was asked why he did not have any documents from the police. He replied that in Panama, there are all robbery cases and no one asks for records because that is really sad. The panel finds that the male claimant did not provide a reasonable explanation for not providing corroborating documents regarding the crimes at his place of business and at his home. According to his evidence, there were at least two incidents where the police took statements: a robbery at his home during which his wife was raped and a robbery at his business during which his relative was killed. The male claimant made no attempt to inquire about getting reports from the police after he came to Canada and made his refugee claim. He was represented by experienced counsel throughout his refugee claim process and has stated at the hearing that he has relatives who reside in Panama, who reasonably could have helped him to inquire about getting reports. The three co-claimants, who are also claimants are citizens of Panama, were educated in that country and are perfectly fluent in the Spanish language. The panel does not find it reasonable that the claimants would make no attempt to get corroborating evidence in the form of police reports. The panel takes a negative inference from the lack of corroborating evidence in this regard.

It is unrealistic to expect in any society that all acts reported to the police, would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. In the case at hand, there is no information to suggest the police have not have made genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimants' allegations and deal with the perpetrators. In fact, documentary evidence30 submitted by the claimants indicates the police do apprehend the perpetrators. Based on the foregoing, I find the claimants have failed to discharge their burden of demonstrating, with clear and convincing evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that the state of Panama would be unable to adequately protect the male claimant and his family members.

The panel notes as well the delay in leaving Panama. The male claimant was asked at the hearing why he and his family had not left Panama much earlier, considering the violence they were experiencing. The male claimant replied that he was working hard to establish himself, that he had children and he wanted to continue his business. He stated that he had children to raise and he chose to remain in Panama until XXXX 2008 when his relative was killed and then when his security guard's gun was stolen in XXXX 2009. The male claimant was asked why he did not apply to come to Canada as an immigrant. He replied that he did not have enough money. He had been told that he did not meet the criteria to apply as an immigrant as he would have needed $400,000 Canadian. The panel finds that the claimants have not provided a reasonable explanation for the long delay in leaving Panama. Their relative was killed at their store in XXXX 2008. The claimants did not leave Panama until one year later in XXXX 2009. The male claimant stated that the incident that caused him to finally decide to leave occurred in XXXX 2009 when the security guard they had hired was robbed of his gun. It was pointed out that he and his family did not leave until XXXX 2009. He stated that he didn't think that far, that he didn't plan and that they just left. It was pointed out to the male claimant that he had not initially mentioned the incident with the security guard in his PIF and that that was only added as an amendment later in the process. He replied that maybe the translator didn't put it in and that the last time he saw his consultant, he was asked if the country was unsteady. He had replied that he had hired a security guard whose gun had been taken away by criminals and they had decided to leave. The panel does not find that that is a reasonable explanation for the initial omission from his PIF of the incident with the security guard. The male claimant signed his PIF Declaration, which states that all the information contained in the form is complete, true and correct. He confirmed at the hearing that his PIF was translated to him before he signed his Declaration. This was the event that finally caused the family to decide to leave Panama and it is not reasonable that the male claimant would not mention it or be aware that it had been omitted from his PIF when he signed it. The panel notes as well that in the form prepared for CIC when he first made his claim for refugee protection, in response to Question #43, which asks why he is asking for Canada's protection, he responded that his family faces death threats from robbers and gangsters. No mention is made of any of the specific incidents noted in male claimant's PIF and at the hearing. The panel finds that the claimants have not provided a reasonable explanation for choosing to remain in a country where they felt that their lives were at risk and the panel takes a negative inference from the delay in leaving Panama.

The claimants spent approximately ten days in the United States before coming to Canada. They did not make a claim for asylum in that country. Their explanation for sojourning in that country was that they could not get a visa for Canada in Panama. They were able to get a visa for the United States and were advised that they could get a Canadian visa once they arrived in the USA. They stated that they did not wish to make a claim for protection in the United States because of the gun violence in that country. The panel does not find this explanation to be plausible, taking into consideration the United State's international human rights reputation and that gun violence does not consistently occur in all areas of the United States. The panel takes a negative inference from the failure to claim asylum in the United States. China

The claimants further explained that they fear being sterilized because of the 'One-Child Policy' if they choose to return to their home province of Guangdong in China due to the fact that they have three children. The panel gave the claimants the opportunity to explain why they think they will be sterilized. While there is evidence of China's poor human rights record, there is also evidence that the Government of China and its constituent provincial authorities, especially Guangdong province, have recognized a pragmatic as well as a social responsibility to change their birth control policies.

The panel notes that documentary evidence indicates in respect of Chinese citizens returning from overseas that:31 Cited in a 2004 report by the Resource Information Center (RIC) of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), a University of California (Irvine) anthropologist who has researched the subject of family planning in China stated that 'in general, people who return to China from abroad are actively welcomed back to the 'motherland,' and children born outside China largely forgiven" (US 21 Jan. 2004). According to an expert on China who lives in Germany, cited in the report on China of the 10th Country of Origin Information Seminar in Budapest, [p]arents responsible for pregnancies or births without permission in China could face ... difficulties .... But Chinese couples living abroad are not bound to the One-Child-Policy. Chinese citizens studying or working in foreign countries can return with more than one child without any serious problem. (ACCORD 17 Mar. 2006, 16) In a 23 October 2008 presentation at the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) of Canada's Calgary office, an associate professor and Mactaggart Research Chair of the China Institute at the University of Alberta likewise noted that Chinese nationals who have children while abroad may not be subject to the One-Child Policy. News sources report that there is an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens who simply pay a fine or travel overseas to have additional children.

As well, country documents32 indicate that a child born out of China, who acquires foreign citizenship, is not included in counts by family planning officials. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants' children born in Panama will not be included in counts by family planning officials. Further to this, should family planning officials choose to assess the claimants in respect of the 'One-Child Policy', documentary evidence pertaining to Article 55 of the 2002 Guangdong family planning regulations, in cases where urban or rural residents have one more child than is permitted, a social support fee will be charged to both the mother and the father.33 The same document goes on to state: While implementation of family planning regulations varies from region to region, a China specialist at the United States (US) Department of State is quoted in a 2004 US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) report as saying that he had received no reports of couples experiencing difficulties upon returning to Fujian and Guangdong after having had children overseas (US 21 Jan. 2004). While country documentary information does not mean that no forced sterilizations have taken place, it appears to be clear that the current trend is to impose fines and forced sterilization or imprisonment is not a probable result of the birth of an out-of-plan child.

In regard to specific incidents of forced abortions or sterilizations in Guangdong province, only one item could be found in reports from sources consulted by the Immigration and Refugee Board Research Directorate.34 The article describes a sterilization plan announced by officials in Puning City, where it was indicated: Officials in Puning are under particular pressure, however: they risk failing in their bid for promotion to a second-tier county if they cannot meet all quotas. That includes keeping the number of births within government limits. The county is under criticism from Guangdong authorities, who want to slow a population growth that is reflecting badly on the entire province. One reason for Puning's large population is that families in the mainly rural region often have up to three or four children.35

The panel notes that there is no evidence before the panel that either the male or female claimants ever resided in Puning and no evidence of forced sterilization in other parts of Guangdong province could be found in all articles consulted by the panel. The preponderance of the evidence indicates that it is more likely than not that a person who has an unauthorized child while living abroad would not face sterilization upon returning to China.36 The panel notes as well that the male claimant is 48 years old and the female claimant is 46 years old. The three co-claimants are all adults and the male and female claimants have not expressed any interest in having additional children.

The panel has given serious consideration to the range of documentary evidence available to the panel and there are mixed messages concerning government policy and action concerning out of plan births. However, on the basis of the totality of the evidence available to the panel in regard to this claim, the panel is persuaded by the documents cited above. The panel finds that the preponderant message from both Chinese government and independent sources is that an enhanced fine rather than forced sterilization or imprisonment is, on a balance of probabilities, the worst outcome that would be faced by the claimants. The panel has also considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines37 with regard to the female claimant's claim. I find no constraint in this regard, that should mitigate my findings noted above.

The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants' subjective fear of persecution in returning to China is not supported by the objective situation in Guangdong province. The panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are not at risk of forced sterilization by family planning officials in Guangdong province. As well, the panel notes the claimants' children (the three co-claimants) are citizens of Panama. The relocation of these children to China is a decision of the parents and is not legally mandated.

The female claimant has alleged that she is a Christian. She has supported that allegation with a Certificate of Baptism from a church in Toronto38 and a letter from her church in Panama.39 She was able to easily answer the questions put to her about her religion. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that she is a Christian.

The male claimant stated at the hearing that he goes to church too. He stated that if he returns to China, he will not have freedom to pursue his beliefs. He was asked what his beliefs are and he stated that he believes in Jesus Christ. He was asked how long he has believed in Jesus Christ. He replied that he has believed for 12 years. He was asked who Jesus Christ is. After much hesitation, he replied that he goes to church but he is not baptized. When he was asked again who Jesus Christ is, he asked the panel to say for him who Jesus Christ is. The male claimant was asked to state who Jesus Christ is a third time. He replied that he went to church and Jesus Christ is a God. He was asked what else he could say about Jesus Christ. He replied that he could not say much but it was in his heart. He was asked why he was not baptized considering that he had been a believer for 12 years. He replied that it was in his heart but his memory was not good, he would have had to write a test and that because he is older, his memory is not good. It was pointed out to the male claimant that he was easily able to respond to questions about his past in Panama and did not appear to have memory problems in that regard. He stated again he was not baptized because his memory was not good. He was asked whether he attended church in Canada or Panama. He replied that he had attended church both in Canada and in Panama every Sunday. It was pointed out to the male claimant that the letter from the church in Panama notes that his wife attended the church but makes no mention of him. He replied that the letter was not for him, he never acquired one and that he just went to church to worship. He was asked why he did not have a letter from the church in Canada or Panama to corroborate his attendance there. He replied that he didn't ask for one. He was asked why he did not. He replied that he did not ask and that he didn't know that he needed it. It was pointed out to the male claimant that he must have known that a corroborating letter was necessary because his wife had provided a letter and her Certificate of Baptism. He replied that he didn't know. The panel finds that the male claimant was not credible in his allegations that he is a Christian. The panel notes that in his PIF, in response to Question #1(h), which asks for a person's religion and denomination, he entered "not applicable". He was extremely hesitant when asked who Jesus Christ is and though he eventually stated that he is a God, he was unable to give any other information about Jesus Christ. He had no corroborating evidence that he had been attending church for 12 years and stated that he didn't know that it was needed. This is not a reasonable explanation, taking into consideration that he was represented by experienced counsel and his wife had provided such supporting documentation in regard to her religious activity. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the male claimant is not presently, nor ever was a Christian.

The panel has considered the situation for Christians in Guangdong province in China. I find that should the claimants return to Guangdong province in China and should they practice Christianity there, there is not a serious possibility that they would be persecuted in Guangdong province for that practice.

The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council recently stated in June 14, 2010 correspondence that the Chinese authorities have demonstrated a high degree of tolerance to Christian activities in general and particularly towards non-registered groups.40 Sources report that many Christian groups, even those which are unregistered, are becoming more public and able to carry out their activities openly.41 ChinaSource is an online resource which assists members of international faith-based communities to work in China. The President of the organization states: [w]hile [reports of persecution] remain a reality of life in China, a survey of the larger picture suggests that they are the exception rather than the rule, and that there may be room for cautious optimism concerning future policy toward China's Christians.42

I also note that according to the documentation, that though there were arrests and incidents of persecution of lay Christians documented in 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009 and 2010, none of these arrests or incidents of persecution were noted as being in Guangdong province. In 2005, there were reports of house church crackdowns in the provinces of Shanxi, Henan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and Jilin and in May 2005, Chinese officials coordinated raids on 100 house churches in Jilin province [northeast China], arresting approximately 600 Christians.43 During the year, there were also reports of similar incidents in Hebei, Xinjiang, Beijing and Shanghai.44 The U.S. 2010 International Religious Freedom Report45 specifically reviews arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China and notes arrests of Christians and incidents of persecution in Beijing, Shanghai, the XUAR, Shandong province, the Xinjiang Autonomous Region, Sichuan province, Anhui province, Henan province, Heilongjiang province, Hebei province and Shanxi province. No mention is made of arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province in the period covered by the report. I have reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and I have found no recent evidence of arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Protestant Christians in Guangdong province.

The Annual Report of Persecution by the Government of China on Christian Churches within mainland China very specifically notes the arrests and incidents of persecution for Christians in China in 2010, but no arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians occurred in Guongdong province where the claimants are from.46 I have reviewed all of the documentary evidence submitted and find no persuasive evidence of recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province.

There is reference to the Liangren church in Guangdong province in several of the documents submitted,47 which note that Pastor Wang Dao, of the Liangren church continues to be harassed by authorities and has been arrested and interrogated several times over the past two years. Documentation suggests that there is heightened interest with this pastor because of his desire to hold large services in pubic places. In this regard, the incidents associated with the Liangren church are distinguished from other underground churches which conduct their services in private settings. In any event, the PSB have only shown interest in the pastor and there is no indication that any lay persons were arrested or have ever been arrested in connection with Liangren church. In addition, the pastor of that church was permitted to submit an application for administrative reconsideration. While it is not known what the results of the administrative reconsideration were, it must be noted that there were no arrests and no one was sentenced as a result of the raid. Further information contained in China Aid Association report48 identifies that a church with 200 members was moved to another district. As well, the same report indicates that three churches were expelled and three Christian schools aborted, however it is not clear why the churches were expelled or why the schools were aborted. It is unclear what the circumstances were that led to the aborting of the schools or what types of churches were expelled or the reason they were expelled. In fact, it is unclear what is meant by the term expelled in this context. What is clear, however, is that no one was arrested in any of these incidents and no one was reported abused. Although country documentary information regarding China generally provides mixed messages concerning the suppression of underground church activity, the lack of any information regarding any instance of arrest and other forms of persecution for Guangdong province, other than the aforementioned incidents, is significant and convincing.

I have considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in China, specifically the articles and reports documenting arrests and incidents of persecution. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Protestant Christians in Guangdong province, there would be some documentation of these arrests or incidents of persecution by reliable sources.

I have considered that the China Aid Association (CAA) has stated in its report and letters that they have not documented all cases of persecution and religious repression occurs in every province in China, including Guangdong and Fujian. However, I note again that there has been no mention at all of recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province, other those cited earlier, in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China and according to the U.S. Department of State International Freedom of Religion Report,49 the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country. In some regions government supervision of religious activity was minimal with registered and unregistered churches existing openly and receiving similar treatment by the authorities.50 In parts of the country, unregistered groups with hundreds of members met openly with the knowledge of local authorities.51 Freedom to participate in religious activities continued to increase in many areas. Religious activity grew not only among the five main religions, but also among the Eastern Orthodox Church and folk religions.52 Some unregistered religious groups had significant membership, properties, financial resources, and networks.53 In parts of the country, unregistered groups grew rapidly and the authorities did not pressure them to register. Although SARA does not officially acknowledge the existence of house churches, its website states that family and friends holding meetings at home (as distinct from formal worship services in public venues) need not register with the Government (the 'Family and Friend Worship Policy').54 Sources report that many Christian groups, even those which are unregistered, are becoming more public and able to carry out their activities openly and operate more or less freely.55 I find that the situation in Guangdong province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests and persecution of ordinary Christians.

The British Home Office Report notes that there are fifty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China who practice without state sanction and that only twenty million practice their religion in state approved churches.56 That report also states that prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families need not register with authorities.57 The British Home Office Report notes that 31.4% of Chinese nationals aged sixteen and older are religious.58

I have considered that the claimants are from Guangdong province, where there have been no reported arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians. I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence and find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants would be able to practice Christianity in a church of their choice if they were to return to Guangdong province in China and that there is not a serious possibility that day would be persecuted for doing so.

The panel is supported in this decision by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.59 This decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong province. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin60 concerning Fujian province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province it would have been documented. In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang61 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely. Justice O'Keefe found in Gong Dao Yao62 that the Board's assessment of the evidence in regard to insufficient details about the destruction of home churches and conclusions based on that evidence were within the range of possible acceptable outcomes.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings, I find that the claimants have not satisfied their burden of establishing a serious possibility that they would be persecuted or that they would be personally subjected to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China or in Panama.
The panel has found that the male and female claimants are excluded pursuant to section 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees.
The three co-claimants are citizens of Panama. Their citizenship allows them to return to their country of origin and seek protection from the state, which the panel has found is available to them.

Alternatively the panel has considered all three protection grounds under section 96 and sub-section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, finds that there is not a serious possibility that the male and female claimants would be persecuted in Panama or in China, nor that they would be subjected personally to a risk to their lives, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

The panel finds that all five claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects their claims. "L.S. Hart" L.S.
